rules.title: Urgency or artificial deadline
rules.why: Attackers manufacture time pressure so victims act before thinking. Legitimate organisations rarely impose same-day deadlines in email.
rules.advice: Slow down. Verify the claim through the organisation's official website or app, not through the message.

values: before the end of the day

examples: Your account will be suspended within 24 hours unless you verify.
FINAL NOTICE: act now to avoid closure.
falsePositives: Transactional alerts such as 'your OTP expires in 10 minutes' are legitimate but may match.

rules.title: Threat of account closure, suspension or legal action
rules.why: Threatening loss of access, money or legal consequences is the standard lever for panic. Real providers usually warn before suspending, and never by surprise email alone.
rules.advice: Do not act from the message. Log in through the official app or website to check the real status of your account.

values: if we do not hear from you

examples: Your account will be blocked today
Failure to comply will result in legal action.
falsePositives: Dunning / collections emails from real vendors contain this language; weigh alongside sender authentication.

rules.title: Request for secrecy or an unusual communication channel
rules.why: Asking the recipient to keep things quiet, or to move to a personal address/phone, is a hallmark of business email compromise. Legitimate business does not require secrecy from colleagues.
rules.advice: Treat any request for confidentiality about money or credentials as a red flag; confirm in person or on a known number.
examples: Please don't tell anyone about this yet, I'm in a meeting - only reply by email.
falsePositives: HR/legal matters sometimes legitimately require confidentiality; check the sender out of band.

rules.title: Unexpected reward, refund or winnings
rules.why: Offers of unexpected money are a classic hook because they create excitement and lower scrutiny. Legitimate schemes do not arrive as surprise emails requesting details.
rules.advice: If you did not enter something, you did not win it. Do not pay any 'processing fee' or hand over bank details.

values: you are eligible for a refund

examples: You have won Rs. 25,00,000 in the lucky draw - claim now!
falsePositives: Retail loyalty offers and genuine refund notifications; check sender and existing orders.

rules.title: Generic, non-personalised greeting
rules.why: A provider you actually use usually knows your name. 'Dear Customer' suggests a bulk mailing that does not know who you are.
rules.advice: A weak signal on its own, but combined with others it supports the phishing read.
examples: Dear Customer, we have noticed unusual activity...
falsePositives: Many legitimate bulk mailings use generic greetings.

rules.title: Fake security alert
rules.why: Claiming an unusual sign-in, unauthorised access or a security issue is a common pretext to get you to click a 'verify' or 'secure account' link.
rules.advice: Check sign-in activity from the official app/site directly. Do not use the link in the email.

values: your account may be at risk

examples: We detected an unusual sign-in to your account. Verify your identity now.
falsePositives: Real security alerts exist; a genuine one tells you to open the app rather than click a link.
